answer:
HYPOTHESIS (final answer to "At what Socioeconomic levels is the advantage in completion rates for Black students more pronounced?"):

The Black advantage in BA-completion rates — where it exists at all — is concentrated at the TOP of the socioeconomic distribution. Raw rates show that Black respondents trail non-Black respondents at every SES level below the top: the Black-vs-non-Black gap is most negative in the low-to-middle SES deciles (e.g., decile 2: 0.66% vs 3.47%, −2.8 pp; decile 7: 1.56% vs 4.89%, −3.3 pp), the gap shrinks steadily as SES rises (unadjusted continuous-interaction logistic model: Black×SES log-odds gradient +0.48 per SD, p = 0.10), and it crosses zero and becomes positive only in the top SES decile, where Black respondents (6.10%, 5/82) actually out-complete non-Black respondents (4.78%, 38/795; +1.3 pp, 95% CI −4.1 to +6.7 pp). Crucially, once academic preparation (ASVAB composite, class percentile), sex, and family size are controlled, the picture sharpens: the Black-vs-non-Black completion gap becomes positive above the median SES and is most pronounced — and statistically significant — in the upper SES range, around the 75th–95th SES percentiles (adjusted log-odds gap ≈ +0.67 at the 75th percentile, z = +2.3, p < 0.05; ≈ +0.92 at the 95th percentile, z = +2.5, p < 0.05). Hypothesis: the Black completion advantage is most pronounced at high socioeconomic levels — top decile on raw rates, and (after adjusting for ability and class rank, which otherwise mask it) robustly across the upper half of the SES distribution, roughly the 75th–95th SES percentiles — while at low-to-mid SES Black respondents face a completion disadvantage.

payload.hypothesis: The Black advantage in BA-completion rates is most pronounced at the highest socioeconomic levels: raw rates show the Black-vs-non-Black gap turning positive only in the top SES decile (6.10% vs 4.78%, +1.3 pp), and after adjusting for ASVAB ability, class percentile, sex, and family size, the Black gap is positive above the median SES and largest and statistically significant around the 75th–95th SES percentiles. At low-to-mid SES Black respondents show a completion disadvantage (most negative gaps in deciles 2-3 and 7), which ability adjustment largely explains; the high-SES advantage persists beyond preparation. Findings are sensitive to binning (no positive gap bin at quartile resolution) and rest on rare events (~28 Black completers overall, ~5 in the top decile), so the top-level crossover itself is not individually significant (Fisher p=0.59); the support for the hypothesis is the monotonic SES gradient across bins, not any single cell.
payload.workflow: 1) Inspected data/nls_ses_processed.csv (8,773 rows, no missingness; SES continuous standardized, no documented bands). 2) Binned SES into pooled deciles (primary), quartiles and quintiles (sensitivity). 3) Computed raw BA-completion rates for Black, White, Hispanic, and pooled non-Black per bin with 95% normal-approx CIs on the difference and per-decile Fisher exact tests. 4) Fit logistic regressions: (a) BA ~ Black x (SES + SES^2) continuous interaction, unadjusted and adjusted for standardized ASVAB composite, class percentile, sex, family size — chosen after a pooled Black x decile-dummy model exhibited complete separation (zero Black events in the bottom decile); (b) Firth penalized logistic per decile for bias-reduced bin-level gaps. 5) Compared raw and adjusted gap gradients side by side and located where the Black advantage is largest/positive. Scripts: analysis_nls_ses.py, analysis_nls_ses_models.py, firth_check.py; tables in outputs/.
